source.title: Exploring the Vulnerability of Deep Neural Networks: A Study of Parameter Corruption
source.authors: Xu Sun; Zhiyuan Zhang; Xuancheng Ren; Ruixuan Luo; Liangyou Li

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains networks to resist gradient-based parameter corruption and reports test-set performance, bearing on the broader question of properties related to generalization. Its corruption measure and outcome differ from the listed version claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports parameter-corruption effects and test accuracy after corruption-resistant training. It does not test random-label memorization, width, convolutional versus fully connected generalization, optimizer or batch-size comparisons, dropout, the magnitude-aware measure in V7, or removal of memorized examples.
record.test_reason: The study measures parameter-corruption vulnerability and evaluates its own corruption-resistant training method. None of V1–V8 is tested. In particular, its absolute-norm perturbations and clean test scores do not measure V7's magnitude-scaled sharpness, training–test gaps, or comparative ranking of generalization measures. Component vulnerability comparisons also do not test V3's architecture-level generalization claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that gradient-based corruption exposes parameter vulnerabilities more effectively than random corruption, and that their corruption-resistant training improves robustness and clean held-out performance. They interpret the latter as suggesting better generalization; they do not establish V7's magnitude-aware sharpness–gap relationship.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses gradient-based parameter corruption and adversarial corruption-resistant training; it does not reproduce the methods in the listed claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that accuracy is approximately unimodal in the magnitude of virtual parameter corruption: small magnitudes can improve clean accuracy, while excessive magnitudes harm learning and reduce clean accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Corruption-resistant training improves clean performance on all five reported tasks: CIFAR-10 accuracy 94.26 to 96.12, Tiny-ImageNet accuracy 66.56 to 67.06, language-model PPL 70.09 to 68.28, parsing UAS 87.26 to 87.89, and translation BLEU 35.33 to 35.69.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Suitably configured adversarial parameter-corruption training can improve clean held-out performance on these benchmark tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: With the corrected Table 2 columns, proposed training outperforms baseline training at every reported corruption magnitude on all five tasks, although severe corruption still substantially degrades some models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial corruption-resistant training improves robustness to the tested absolute-L2 parameter perturbations.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient-based corruption produces much greater degradation than random corruption, and component comparisons identify particularly vulnerable normalization parameters. These results concern corruption vulnerability rather than generalization gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-based parameter perturbations expose vulnerabilities that random perturbations often miss.

record.problems: Table 2 reports a small set of benchmark models and conditions without uncertainty estimates; the corruption tests use constructed parameter perturbations, and ImageNet experiments use Tiny-ImageNet for corruption-resistant training.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1, Figure 3, and Appendix Tables 3–5 report additional corruption effects on accuracy, loss, or task metrics, including separate random and gradient-based perturbations and component- or layer-specific conditions. They were left out because they report parameter-corruption vulnerability rather than a listed generalization-gap version, and the selected rows already capture the study's corruption-resistant-training results.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width sweeps past the width required for zero training error.
Held-out performance comparisons between convolutional and fully connected image classifiers, including locality and initialization effects.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons and tuning-dependent differences.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove their penalty.
Dropout ablations, training-set-size dependence, and removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance versus training–test error gaps among comparably fitted networks, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing examples selected by memorization influence versus random removal.

record.verdict_notes: All 30 rows report the study's own method performance and should remain outside V1–V8. States are cannot_determine relative to those versions, rather than judgments about whether the method improves performance. Table 2's flattened text interleaves columns, causing substantial extraction errors in R14–R18, R20–R24, and R26–R30. Additional vulnerability experiments are already declared in rows_left_out and do not require missing entries for any listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image generalization.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization comparisons.
Large-batch effects under fixed epoch budgets.

The study measures gradient-based loss and accuracy changes under parameter corruption, but does not use weight-magnitude-scaled perturbations, compare train and test error gaps among similarly trained networks, or rank sharpness against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing examples selected by memorization influence.
